definition:
The Bible never argues God into existence; it introduces him. Its first sentence assumes him, “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1), and the rest of Scripture is the long disclosure of who he is. The God of the Bible is the one living God, the maker of everything that exists. He is not part of the world he made, not one more being inside it, however large, and yet he is present to every part of it and nearer to each creature than it is to itself. Theologians call these two truths transcendence (God is above and beyond creation) and immanence (God is present within it); Scripture holds them together, as when God says he dwells “in a high and holy place, and with the oppressed and humble in spirit” (Isaiah 57:15). He is personal: he speaks, chooses, loves, grieves, and keeps promises. He names himself to Moses as the LORD, the one who is and who remains faithful, and the Christian church confesses that this one God has made himself fully known in Jesus Christ as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The doctrine of the Trinity, God's attributes, and his names each have their own study; this one traces the basic confession that there is one God and asks who he is.

The common Hebrew word for God is 'elohim. It is plural in form, but when it refers to Israel's God it takes singular verbs, and most grammarians explain the plural as one of majesty or fullness rather than as a hint of several gods or a direct statement of the Trinity. The shorter 'el is the general Semitic word for a god, often combined in titles such as 'el 'elyon, ‘God Most High’ (Genesis 14:19). God's personal name is the four letters YHWH, which Jewish reverence stopped pronouncing and replaced in reading with 'adonai, ‘Lord’; most English Bibles print it as LORD in small capitals. In the Greek Old Testament and the New Testament, God is theos, and the name YHWH is rendered kyrios, ‘Lord’, which is why it matters so much when the apostles call Jesus kyrios.
ot:
Genesis presents God as the maker of heaven and earth before it presents him as anything else. The creation account of Genesis 1 is sparing: there is no battle among gods, no divine family, no raw material that resists him. The sun and moon, which Israel's neighbors worshiped, are simply lights he made. The patriarchs know God as the one who calls and promises. Melchizedek blesses Abram by “God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth” (Genesis 14:19); God appears to Abram as “God Almighty” (Genesis 17:1); Abraham calls on “the LORD, the Eternal God” (Genesis 21:33). The God of Genesis is not a local deity tied to one shrine. He goes with Abraham from Ur to Canaan, with Jacob to Haran, and with Joseph into Egypt.

At the burning bush God gives his name. Moses asks what to say when the Israelites ask the name of the God of their fathers, and God answers, “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14), then names himself the LORD, “My name forever” (Exodus 3:15). The Hebrew 'ehyeh 'asher 'ehyeh can be rendered ‘I am who I am’ or ‘I will be who I will be’; interpreters have heard in it God's self-existence, his freedom from definition by anything outside himself, and his promise to be present and faithful in what follows. The Greek translation rendered it ‘I am the one who is’, which shaped later theology deeply. The exodus then shows who this God is by what he does. The Ten Commandments begin not with an argument but with an identity: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). Because of who he is, Israel must have no other gods before him and make no image of him. At Sinai God proclaims his own character, compassionate and gracious, slow to anger (Exodus 34:6-7), the self-description the rest of the Old Testament quotes more than any other.

Deuteronomy states the confession that shaped Israel and later the church. “You were shown these things so that you would know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides Him” (Deuteronomy 4:35). Then comes the Shema, named for its first Hebrew word, ‘hear’: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4). The Hebrew can also be rendered ‘the LORD is our God, the LORD alone’, and scholars debate which is meant; either way, the verse binds Israel to one God and calls for love with all the heart, soul, and strength. The Old Testament often speaks of other gods, as when Exodus asks, “Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?” (Exodus 15:11), or when Psalm 82 pictures God judging “among the gods” in the divine assembly. Scholars read this language differently. Some, such as Mark S. Smith, argue that Israel's faith developed over centuries from the worship of one God among many to the strict monotheism of Isaiah 40 to 48. Others argue that these texts speak of real but created spiritual beings or of the gods of the nations as rivals already judged, and that the LORD was never one god among equals. All agree that by the exile the prophets were saying without qualification that he alone is God.

The historical books and the prophets show the living God against the idols. On Mount Carmel in the ninth century BC Elijah challenged Israel to stop wavering between the LORD and Baal, and the people fell facedown crying, “The LORD, He is God” (1 Kings 18:39). Solomon, dedicating the temple around 960 BC, confessed that “heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built” (1 Kings 8:27). The Psalms mock idols that have mouths but cannot speak and add that “Those who make them become like them” (Psalm 115:8), while Psalm 139 confesses a God from whose presence there is no escape. Isaiah 40 to 48, addressed to exiles in Babylon, is the Old Testament's fullest statement of who God is. It asks, “To whom will you liken God?” (Isaiah 40:18), and answers that he is the everlasting Creator who calls the stars by name, the first and the last, besides whom there is no God (Isaiah 44:6), who alone can announce what is to come. He says, “Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other” (Isaiah 45:22). Jeremiah calls him “the true God; He is the living God and eternal King” (Jeremiah 10:10), and Malachi grounds Israel's survival in his constancy: “I, the LORD, do not change” (Malachi 3:6).
nt:
Jesus stood entirely within Israel's confession. Asked for the greatest commandment, he quoted the Shema, “Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One” (Mark 12:29), and he taught his disciples to pray to “Our Father in heaven” (Matthew 6:9). He told the Samaritan woman that “God is Spirit” (John 4:24), meaning not that God is a vapor but that he is not bound to a place or a body, so that true worship is not tied to Gerizim or Jerusalem. In his prayer before the cross he called the Father “the only true God” and set himself beside him: eternal life is to know “the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent” (John 17:3). The Gospels show the one God of Israel acting in Jesus, forgiving sins, calming the sea, and receiving worship, and they present Jesus as the Son who alone knows and reveals the Father.

The apostles preached the one God to Jews and Gentiles in different ways. To pagans at Lystra, Paul and Barnabas announced “the living God, who made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them” (Acts 14:15). In Athens Paul told philosophers that the God who made the world “does not live in temples made by human hands” and is not served “as if He needed anything” (Acts 17:24-25), and he quoted their own poets to say that in him we live and move and have our being (Acts 17:28). Paul's letters show that pagan converts had “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9). Romans 1 explains idolatry as the refusal of what God has made known, exchanging “the glory of the immortal God for images” (Romans 1:23), and Romans 11 ends in praise: “For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things” (Romans 11:36).

The most striking thing the New Testament does with the doctrine of God is to include Jesus within it without abandoning one God. In 1 Corinthians 8:6 Paul restates the Shema: “yet for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist.” The words God and Lord from Deuteronomy 6:4 are divided between the Father and Jesus, and Jesus is placed on the Creator's side of the line. In Philippians 2:9-11 Paul takes Isaiah 45:23, where the one God swears that every knee will bow to him, and says every knee will bow at the name of Jesus, “to the glory of God the Father.” Scholars such as Larry Hurtado and Richard Bauckham have argued that this worship of Jesus within strict Jewish monotheism appeared very early, not as a slow later development. The New Testament never solves the resulting question with a formula; the church's doctrine of the Trinity is its answer.

The apostles also say what God is like in a few short sentences that have shaped Christian thought. “God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5); “God is love” (1 John 4:8, 16); he is the “Father of the heavenly lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow” (James 1:17); he is “the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, the only God” (1 Timothy 1:17) who “dwells in unapproachable light” (1 Timothy 6:16). James warns that believing “that God is one” is not enough, since even the demons believe it (James 2:19); knowing God means trusting and obeying him. Hebrews says that whoever comes to God must believe “that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him” (Hebrews 11:6). The Bible ends with the heavenly worship of the God who created all things (Revelation 4:11) and with the promise that “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3). The God who could not be contained by the temple at last dwells with his people.

keyTexts.why: The Bible's first sentence introduces God as the Creator of everything. It assumes his existence and sets him apart from all he made.
God gives Moses his name: I AM WHO I AM, the LORD. The center of the Old Testament's disclosure of who God is.
God identifies himself by what he has done in bringing Israel out of slavery, and forbids other gods and images.
The Shema: the LORD is one, and he is to be loved with all the heart, soul, and strength. Israel's central confession, quoted by Jesus.
Even the highest heaven cannot contain God. Solomon's prayer holds God's transcendence and his willingness to dwell with his people together.
Elijah's contest with the prophets of Baal. The living God acts; the idol is silent.
From everlasting to everlasting, God is God. He was before the world and does not depend on it.
To whom will you liken God? The incomparable Creator who calls the stars by name and does not grow weary.
I am the LORD, and there is no other. The Old Testament's clearest statement of monotheism, addressed to the nations.
Jesus names the Shema as the greatest commandment, standing within Israel's faith in the one God.
God is Spirit. He is not bound to a place or a body, and true worship is not tied to a single mountain or temple.
Paul tells the Athenians that the Creator needs nothing from human hands and that in him all live and move and have their being.
Paul restates the Shema with one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ. Jesus is included within the identity of the one God.
God alone is immortal and dwells in unapproachable light. The New Testament's confession of God's transcendence.
God is love. A short confession of God's character that the church has read in light of the Father's gift of the Son.

history:
The early church confessed the one God of Israel against two opponents. Against Greek and Roman polytheism, second-century apologists such as Justin Martyr argued that there is one Creator and that the gods of the cities were not gods. Against Marcion, who taught around 144 that the Creator of the Old Testament was a lesser, merely just god distinct from the good Father revealed by Jesus, the church insisted that the Creator and the Father of Jesus are the same God. Irenaeus of Lyon, writing around 180, made this his central theme, and Theophilus of Antioch and Irenaeus stated plainly that God created from nothing, not from eternal matter. The creeds open with this confession. The baptismal creed of the church at Rome, the ancestor of the Apostles' Creed, began with belief in God the Father almighty, and the Nicene Creed (325, expanded at Constantinople in 381) begins with belief in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth and of all things visible and invisible.

The church's theologians then asked what it means to call God one and Creator. Augustine, in his Confessions (around 397 to 400), described God as more inward to him than his own inmost self and higher than his highest. Gregory of Nyssa and the writer known as Pseudo-Dionysius (around 500) stressed that God surpasses every concept, so that we know him truly but never comprehend him. Anselm of Canterbury in the Proslogion (1077 to 1078) described God as the being than which nothing greater can be thought. Thomas Aquinas in the Summa Theologiae (begun around 1265) offered five ways of reasoning from the world to God and taught that God is simple, not composed of parts, and that his essence is his existence; he read Exodus 3:14 as teaching that ‘He who is’ is God's most fitting name. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) confessed one true God, Creator of all things, and taught that no likeness between Creator and creature can be noted without a greater unlikeness.

The Reformers kept this doctrine of God and put it to work. John Calvin opened his Institutes (final edition 1559) by saying that nearly all true wisdom consists in knowing God and knowing ourselves. The Westminster Confession (1646) and its Shorter Catechism (1647) described God as a Spirit, infinite, eternal, and unchangeable in his being, wisdom, power, holiness, justice, goodness, and truth. At the same time others pressed on the distance between philosophy and faith: Blaise Pascal's private memorial of his conversion in 1654 contrasted the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob with the God of the philosophers.

The modern period challenged the doctrine from several sides. Baruch Spinoza's Ethics (1677) identified God with nature. Deists such as Matthew Tindal (Christianity as Old as the Creation, 1730) kept a Creator but removed revelation and miracle. Ludwig Feuerbach's The Essence of Christianity (1841) argued that God is a projection of human ideals. Christian theology answered in several ways. Karl Barth's commentary on Romans (second edition 1922) stressed the infinite difference between God and humanity. Process theologians following Alfred North Whitehead (Process and Reality, 1929) and Charles Hartshorne described a God who changes with the world. Jürgen Moltmann's The Crucified God (1972) argued that God suffers in Christ. Open theists, beginning with The Openness of God (1994), argued that God does not know the free future exhaustively. In recent decades many theologians have argued for a retrieval of classical theism. The site's full treatments at /theology/doctrine/god-and-trinity and /theology/doctrine/divine-attributes survey these questions.

differ.body: God is the perfect, self-existent being, dependent on nothing, not composed of parts (simple), unchanging in his being, and not subject to suffering in his divine nature. Scripture's language of God's regret, anger, or changing his mind is true speech accommodated to human understanding, just as its language of God's arm or eyes is. Defenders, from Augustine and Aquinas to the Reformed and Lutheran confessions and many recent writers, argue that only such a God can be the Creator of all things rather than one more being within the world, and they point to texts such as Malachi 3:6, James 1:17, and 1 Samuel 15:29, which say God does not change or change his mind.

God is eternal, all-powerful, and perfectly good, but the classical account, shaped by Greek philosophy, went further than Scripture requires. God genuinely responds to his creatures, experiences emotions such as grief and joy, and enters into real give-and-take with people in time. Defenders, including many analytic philosophers of religion and some evangelical theologians, point to texts such as Genesis 6:6 and Exodus 32:14, where the LORD grieves and relents, and argue that the Bible's personal portrait of God should govern the philosophical categories rather than the reverse. Some within this view also hold that God suffers with his people and in the cross.

God knows everything that can be known, but the free decisions of creatures do not yet exist to be known, so the future is partly open even for God. God is sovereign, wise enough to meet every possibility, and he has determined some things in advance, but he takes risks in creating free persons. Defenders such as Clark Pinnock, John Sanders, and Gregory Boyd argue that texts in which God tests people to find out what they will do, or changes a declared plan when people repent, should be read as meaning what they say. The view is sharply disputed among evangelicals; many regard it as incompatible with Scripture's teaching on God's foreknowledge, while its defenders consider it a faithful reading within the confession of the one Creator.

errors:
The church has named several errors about who God is. Polytheism, the belief in many gods, is rejected by the whole Bible from the first commandment to the apostles' preaching. Pantheism, which identifies God with the world, denies that he is the Creator distinct from what he made; the Bible's God is not the universe but its maker. Deism, which keeps a Creator who does not act, speak, or intervene, contradicts the living God who spoke at Sinai and raised Jesus from the dead. Marcionism, which divided the God of the Old Testament from the Father of Jesus, was rejected because Jesus himself prayed to the God of Israel as his Father. The Trinity study treats the errors of modalism and tritheism.

Other errors are quieter. One is imagining God as a very large creature, a being within the universe who differs from us only in size or power, so that he competes with his creatures for room. Another is the practical religion the sociologists Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton called moralistic therapeutic deism (2005): a God who exists mainly to help people feel good and be nice, and who does not need to be involved in life unless called on to solve a problem. The Bible's God is neither distant nor domesticated. He is the holy one who cannot be contained and the Father who draws near.
life:
To believe in the God of the Bible is to know that the universe is not an accident and that a person is not alone in it. Everything that exists, including one's own life, depends at every moment on a God who does not need anything and who gives freely. That frees a person from trying to be their own foundation. It also exposes idols: anything trusted, loved, or feared as if it were God, whether money, success, a nation, a relationship, or one's own reputation. The prophets' warning that we become like what we worship applies as much to modern idols as ancient ones.

Knowing God is also the center of prayer and hope. Christians pray to one God who is both above all things and nearer than breath, so they can pray with reverence and with confidence. Their hope rests on his faithfulness, the God who does not change and whose name means he will be present with his people. Jesus called this knowledge of the only true God eternal life, and the Bible's last pages promise that the knowledge will become sight when God himself dwells with his people.
questions: The Ten Commandments begin with God naming himself by what he has done: he brought Israel out of slavery. Why does the Bible introduce God this way rather than by argument?
Paul restates the Shema in 1 Corinthians 8:6 with one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ. What does that show about how the first Christians understood Jesus?
Psalm 115 says those who make idols become like them. What might people today trust or worship in God's place, and how does that shape them?
